column2: We constructed a function whose derivative equals itself. Could a different function obey the same rule and start at the same height? What we just proved does not settle that. The steps reach E, but nothing yet forces every solution to follow our steps.

So build a test. Take any function y that has a derivative, and multiply it by E of minus x. Differentiate that product. One contribution is y prime times E of minus x. The other comes from E of minus x itself, whose slope is minus E of minus x, by the chain rule. Together they make y prime minus y, times E of minus x.

Try it on functions that break the rule. Our degree-two polynomial starts at height one, but its derivative loses its top term. Its product with E of minus x tilts. On these axes, degree four breaks the rule less, and tilts less. E of minus x is never zero, so the product can only be level where y prime equals y. Suppose a function obeys the rule everywhere. What must its product do?

It stays level. One contribution is the proposed function times E of minus x, and the other is its negative. They cancel. A slope of zero across an interval means a constant value, and at zero that value is one. So y of x times E of minus x equals one, everywhere on that interval.

Now multiply both sides by E of x. The product grid already gave us E of x times E of minus x equals one, so the left side collapses to y of x. The proposed solution must equal E of x everywhere on its interval. That is the rule in both directions. E obeys it, and whatever obeys it is E.

Is this a circle? Follow the arrows. The series gave us E prime equals E, by differentiating term by term. Multiplying series in the grid gave us E of x times E of minus x equals one. Neither step used this result. All we added was the product rule, the chain rule, and the fact that zero slope on an interval means constant. No uniqueness theorem and no logarithm came in. Every arrow points one way.

The word interval is doing work. Cut a gap in the domain, and the far piece can be three times E. Its slope equals its height, and the start at zero never hears about it. So the proposed function needs one unbroken interval containing the starting input, with a derivative at every point.

The same test handles any constant rate k. If y prime equals k times y, multiply by E of minus k t. The contributions cancel again, so y of t equals y of zero times E of k t. A positive k grows, a negative k decays, a zero k stays put, and a zero start stays at zero. The rate k has units of one over time, so k t is a pure number, ready to be an input. Whether a real quantity obeys this law is a question for each application.

The power series, the small-multiplier limit and the rate law are three constructions of the same object. Its powers, derivatives and growth rule fit together because they express the same structure from different sides. All three debts are paid.
